newsitem.title: UK: Gold Outlook - Focus sharpens on platinum.
newsitem.headline: Gold Outlook - Focus sharpens on platinum.

text.p: The focus in precious metals has sharpened on platinum and palladium amid prospects of further delays in Russian supplies, while gold remains range-bound after last week's assault.
Platinum prices sea-sawed last week after having shot up by $14.50 to $382.50 an ounce on Thursday following a squeeze in forward rates.
Spot platinum was trading at $380.00 an ounce in early London trading, while NYMEX July platinum futures in New York ended at $377.20 on Friday.

The white metal was spooked by rumours concerning a swap of 30 tonnes of Russian gold supposedly held by Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral against a hard currency loan for platinum and palladium.

Long delays in Russian PGM (platinum group metals) exports have kept the market on tenterhooks for months and players are wary of a squeezes that smacks of difficulty in getting hold of the Russian metal.
Some dealers said platinum could easily move $10 higher or more in the near-term if supply concerns continued.
Sergei Kyshtymov, head of precious metals operations at the Russian Central Bank denied the rumours on Friday, saying there had been "no such talks" with UBS to swap gold for platinum and palladium.

Dealers, however, are not yet convinced. They said the heavy Swiss borrowing that stoked up the forward rates is unusual in a market where supply shortages can be filled from South Africa -- unlike in palladium where exports are almost single handedly controlled by Russia.
The platinum market went into a backwardation with one-month lease rates surging to about 13 percent from 5.5 percent earlier in the week.
But some analysts were cynical about the spiral of prices.
"By Monday, the price may collapse by $20," said one precious metals analyst in London.

"When dealers heard these rumours a lot of people came piling in on the basis that the palladium price had gone roaring up and now it was platinum's turn," he said. "There was an assumption that the platinum market had fallen into concentrated hands."
Players will be guarded against any signs that big producer South Africa would jump in to increase supplies, dealers said.
But activity will be slowed down by the Jewish Passover this week and the Moslem Eid Al-Adha holiday that is likely to stall activity in the Middle East.
Kyshtymov said the Russian government had yet to sign a decree that would allow negotiations the Japan, the biggest buyer of PGM, on contracts for 1997 supplies, already delayed since December.
"We don't know when the deal will be signed," he said.

But on Monday Japanese sources said Russian central bank officials were to meet with several Japanese trading houses in Tokyo to discuss the possible use of gold to back bonds issued by the government.
This is seen as part of a major overhaul of the way Russia's often archaic and always secretive precious metals market is run.
Gold took refuge in the $340-$345 range last week after being slashed to $337.50 an ounce in an aggressive sell-off.

But pessimism about gold's fortunes still persist against a background of possible central bank sales, rising stocks prices, and a benign inflation environment in the United States, with most analysts expecting another thrust to the February low of $336.15 or even lower.
Any moves above $345 likely to be sold into for now,
analysts said.
But bullion may benefit from possible further rises in
the platinum and palladium.
Spot gold closed at $341.10/$341.60 an ounce in New York
on Friday. By 0830 GMT on Monday, it was trading at $342.60/$342.90 in London.
-- Clelia Oziel, London Newsroom +44-171-542 8071
